concepts.text: Alphonse Daudet: French novelist and short-story writer
Background: 1870-71 Franco-Prussian War; Prussia under Bismarck defeated France and took Alsace and Lorraine
Narrated by Franz, a young schoolboy in an Alsace village

sections.name: 1.2 Plot: the morning of the last lesson

concepts.text: Franz is late for school and dreads a test on participles he has not learnt
He is tempted to spend the day outdoors (birds, Prussian soldiers drilling) but hurries to school
Crowd at the bulletin board: news of the past two years (lost battles, orders) came from there
School is unusually quiet; no bustle, Franz expects a scolding but M. Hamel speaks kindly
M. Hamel wears his Sunday best: green coat, frilled shirt, embroidered black silk cap
Village elders (old Hauser with his primer, the former mayor, the former postmaster) sit at the back

sections.name: 1.3 Plot: the order from Berlin and the lesson

concepts.text: M. Hamel announces an order from Berlin: only German to be taught in Alsace and Lorraine schools
This is their last French lesson; the new master arrives tomorrow
Franz regrets wasting time on bird-nests and sliding on the Saar; his books now feel like old friends
M. Hamel blames everyone: parents sent children to work, he himself sent them to water flowers or gave holidays
French is called the most beautiful, clearest and most logical language in the world
A language is like a key to their prison when a people are enslaved
Grammar, writing (new copies 'France, Alsace' like little flags), and history lessons follow; Franz understands everything
Pigeons coo on the roof; Franz wonders whether they too will be made to sing in German
At noon the church clock strikes, Prussian trumpets sound; M. Hamel writes 'Vive La France!' on the board and dismisses them
Franz: careless at first, then remorseful and sensitive
M. Hamel: strict but devoted teacher of forty years; patriotic and emotional
Villagers: regret not learning their language when they could
Importance of mother tongue and linguistic identity
Linguistic chauvinism and the imposition of a language by conquerors
Procrastination: putting off learning till tomorrow
Patriotism, loss of freedom and the pain of war
First-person narration; irony (the last lesson becomes the best lesson)
Symbolism: pigeons, the bulletin board, 'Vive La France!'
Pathos and vivid description
Infer meanings: in great dread of, counted on, thumbing the pages, a great bustle, reproach ourselves with
Word origins (etymology) of words like tycoon, tulip, logo, zero, trek
Choosing correct meanings of words from context
Think as you read: what Franz expected; what was unusual; what was on the bulletin board; changes the order caused; Franz's changing feelings
Understanding the text: how people realised the value of their language; meaning of the pigeons' remark
Talking about the text: peoples who lost their languages; linguistic minorities' problems; can pride in language go too far (linguistic chauvinism)
Past perfect tense to show an earlier past action (e.g. 'I had counted on...')
Short answers (40-50 words) on M. Hamel and Franz; long answers on the importance of mother tongue

sections.name: 2.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Anees Jung: Indian journalist and writer; extract from 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'
Two-part reportage on child labour and poverty

sections.name: 2.2 Part 1: 'Sometimes I find a fortune in the garbage' (Saheb)

concepts.text: Saheb-e-Alam: a ragpicker boy whose family left Dhaka (Bangladesh) after storms swept away their fields and homes
He lives in Seemapuri, a slum on the outskirts of Delhi; families live in mud structures with tin and tarpaulin roofs
Ragpicking is a means of survival; for children garbage is wrapped in wonder (they may find a coin)
Many children go barefoot; walking barefoot is explained as tradition but is really poverty
Saheb's name means 'lord of the universe', an irony given his condition
The author jokingly offers to open a school; he later asks if the school is ready
Saheb later works at a tea stall for 800 rupees and meals, carrying a steel canister instead of a plastic bag
He loses his freedom: he is no longer his own master

sections.name: 2.3 Part 2: 'I want to drive a car' (Mukesh)

concepts.text: Mukesh lives in Firozabad, the centre of India's glass-bangle industry
About 20,000 children work in high-temperature furnaces and glass-blowing, often losing their eyesight
Child labour is illegal yet thrives; families have made bangles for generations
Savita, a young girl, solders bits of glass; bangles symbolise a married woman's auspiciousness
An elderly woman says she has not had enough to eat in her life though she has made bangles
The vicious circle: sahukars, middlemen, policemen, bureaucrats and politicians keep the workers poor
Fear of the police and the lack of a cooperative prevent the workers from organising
Mukesh dreams of becoming a motor mechanic, a dream that breaks with tradition
Child labour and the loss of childhood ('lost spring')
Poverty, exploitation and the burden of tradition and fate (karam)
Hope and dreams of a better future
Reportage with dialogue and vivid imagery
Irony (Saheb's name, the bangles' bright colours against grim lives)
Title metaphor: spring as childhood
Think as you read: what Saheb looks for in garbage; why he lives in Seemapuri; why children walk barefoot; whether Saheb is happy at the tea stall
Understanding the text: Mukesh's dream; hazards of the bangle industry; why the workers cannot organise
Talking about the text: the role of the government and society in ending child labour
Short answers on Saheb and Mukesh; long answer on child labour

sections.name: 3.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: William O. Douglas: Judge of the US Supreme Court and environmentalist; extract from 'Of Men and Mountains'
Autobiographical first-person account of a childhood fear of water and how he conquered it
At three or four, waves at a California beach knocked him down and buried him; the first fear of water
At ten or eleven he decided to learn to swim at the Yakima YMCA pool, using water wings at first
The shallow end was about three feet deep and the deep end nine feet
A big bruiser of a boy, about eighteen, picked him up and tossed him into the deep end
He planned to spring up from the bottom but sank; he rose and sank three times
Panic and stark terror; legs paralysed; he tried to scream but no sound came
Finally he stopped struggling, felt peace and blacked out; he woke beside the pool, vomiting
A haunting fear of water stayed for years; his legs would freeze whenever he entered water
The fear returned when he waded in the Tieton or Bumping River or bathed in Warm Lake, spoiling fishing, canoeing, boating and swimming
He resolved to conquer the fear because it was ruining his enjoyment of life
He hired an instructor who trained him for months, several days a week, an hour a day
The instructor used a rope tied to a belt around him, running through a pulley on an overhead cable
Step-by-step training: face under water to exhale, nose up to inhale; kicking with legs; then a whole stroke
Even after training, traces of terror remained when he swam alone
He tested himself at Lake Wentworth, New Hampshire: dived off a dock and swam two miles across the lake
At Warm Lake he dived in, swam across and back, and shouted with joy that the terror was gone
Fear can paralyse but can be overcome through willpower and practice
'All we have to fear is fear itself' (Franklin D. Roosevelt's words, quoted by the author)
The will to live, and the peace felt at the edge of death
The freedom that follows victory over fear
Vivid sensory description of panic; repetition and suspense in the drowning scene
Reflective tone; contrast between helplessness and triumph
Words and phrases: bruiser, flailed, paralysed, misadventure, stark terror, vestiges of fear, residual doubt
Think as you read: the 'misadventure'; what he planned to do when thrown in; how the experience affected him
Understanding the text: why he was determined to overcome the fear; how the instructor built a swimmer; how he tested that the fear was gone
Why Douglas says 'All we have to fear is fear itself'; how the near-death experience shaped him
Talking about the text: fears you have overcome; how fear holds people back
Short answers on the YMCA incident and the training method
Long answer: courage and determination in overcoming fear
Extract-based MCQs on the drowning scene

sections.name: 4.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Selma Lagerlöf: Swedish writer, first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1909)
Story set in the iron-mining area of Värmland, Sweden
A poor peddler sells handmade rattraps, begs and steals to survive
He thinks the world is a rattrap: riches and joys are baits that trap people
An old crofter welcomes him, gives him food and porridge, plays cards (mjölis) with him
The crofter shows him thirty kronor earned from his cow's milk; the peddler later steals it
He gets lost in the forest and realises he himself is caught in the rattrap
At the Ramsjö ironworks the ironmaster mistakes him for an old comrade, Captain von Stahle
He declines the invitation; the ironmaster's daughter Edla Willmansson persuades him to come
After he is bathed and shaved the ironmaster realises his mistake and wants to send him away
Edla insists he stay for Christmas Eve; he is treated kindly
He leaves a rattrap with the thirty kronor and a letter for the crofter, signed Captain von Stahle
Peddler: poor, bitter, but redeemed by kindness
Edla: compassionate and mature; her goodness transforms him
Ironmaster: impulsive and proud
Crofter: lonely and trusting
The world as a rattrap: temptation and greed
Human goodness and the power of kindness to redeem
Loneliness and the need for companionship
Extended metaphor of the rattrap; irony; humour
Symbolism of the rattrap and the Christmas gift
Infer meanings: keep body and soul together, plods along, unwonted joy, nodded a haughty consent, fallen into a line of thought
Labels for the peddler: vagabond, stranger, tramp, ragamuffin, guest
Words for weary movement: lurch, stumble, slog, trudge, plod
Ironworks terms: hammer strokes, pig iron, coal dust, anvil
Reflexive pronouns: emphasis and reference to the subject
Think as you read: source of the rattrap idea; why he was amused; why the crofter was talkative; why he declined and accepted the invitation
Understanding the text: how the peddler interpreted kindness; difference between the ironmaster and Edla; the peddler's change
Talking about the text: the world as a rattrap; how loneliness affects people
Short answers on Edla and the peddler; long answer on kindness

sections.name: 5.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Louis Fischer: American journalist; extract from 'The Life of Mahatma Gandhi'
Narrates Gandhi's Champaran movement (1917)
Rajkumar Shukla, a sharecropper from Champaran (Bihar), meets Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress (December 1916)
He persists, following Gandhi to Cawnpore and Ahmedabad until Gandhi agrees
They go to Calcutta, then Patna; at Rajendra Prasad's house the servants think Gandhi an untouchable
At Muzaffarpur, Professor J.B. Kripalani and lawyers receive him
Tinkathia system: sharecroppers had to grow indigo on 15% (3/20) of their land and give it to the landlords
When Germany produced synthetic indigo, landlords demanded compensation to release peasants
Gandhi met the landlords' association and the British commissioner; he was told to leave

sections.name: 5.4 Gandhi at Motihari and civil disobedience

concepts.text: Gandhi went to Motihari; he was served a notice to leave Champaran
He refused, following the 'higher law of our being, the voice of conscience'
Thousands of peasants gathered at the court; the government dropped the case
First civil disobedience in modern India succeeded
Commission of inquiry formed; Gandhi accepted 25% refund
The amount mattered less than the landlords' surrender of money and prestige
Within a few years the planters abandoned their estates
Gandhi started schools in villages with Kasturba, his son Devdas and Mahadev Desai
A doctor gave medical aid (castor oil, quinine, sulphur ointment); sanitation was taught
Gandhi refused C.F. Andrews's help to teach self-reliance
Self-reliance and courage in the freedom struggle
Civil disobedience and non-violence
Peasants' rights and freedom from fear
Think as you read: Shukla's persistence; why Gandhi accepted 25%; the impact on the peasants
Understanding the text: why the Champaran episode was a turning point in Gandhi's life
Talking about the text: civil disobedience today
Short answers on the tinkathia system; long answer on self-reliance

sections.name: 6.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Asokamitran: Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios, Madras, in the 1940s-50s; extract from 'My Years with Boss'
Humorous memoir; 'the Boss' is S.S. Vasan, founder of Gemini Studios
Pancake: the brand of make-up material bought by the truckload for actors
The make-up room was in a building said to have been Robert Clive's stables
Hot, glaring lights and mirrors made it like a torture chamber for actors
Make-up staff showed 'national integration': Bengali chief, Maharashtrian, Kannadiga, Andhra, Indian Christian, Anglo-Burmese and local Tamils
Strict hierarchy: the chief made up main actors, assistants the lesser ones, the office boy the crowd players

sections.name: 6.3 The office boy and Kothamangalam Subbu

concepts.text: The office boy had come hoping to be a star actor, writer, director or lyricist; he stayed frustrated
He blamed Kothamangalam Subbu, the No. 2 at Gemini, for his failure
Subbu: poet and loyal aide of the Boss, cheerful, able to suggest many ways to shoot a scene
Subbu wrote poetry and a novel ('Thillana Mohanambal'), acted well, and supported many dependants
The legal adviser, nicknamed 'the opposition', wore pants, tie and coat
He once recorded an actress's angry outburst and played it back; she was stunned and her career ended

sections.name: 6.5 The author's job and the story department

concepts.text: The author's job was cutting and filing newspaper clippings; others thought he did nothing
The story department of writers and poets was eventually closed

sections.name: 6.6 Moral Re-Armament Army and the English poet

concepts.text: Gemini Studios was anti-communist; the Boss welcomed the Moral Re-Armament Army in 1952
About two hundred MRA members staged 'Jotham Valley' and 'The Forgotten Factor'; Tamil drama later copied their sunrise and sunset scenes
An English poet visited the studio and spoke; nobody understood him and his identity remained a mystery
Years later the author found he was Stephen Spender, editor of 'The Encounter'
Spender contributed to 'The God That Failed', essays by ex-communists such as Gide, Silone, Koestler, Richard Wright and Louis Fischer
Humour, irony and gentle satire on the film industry
Self-deprecating humour of the author
Cultural gap between an English poet and Tamil film workers; anti-communism of the era
Irony, understatement and mock-heroic description
Anecdotal structure and caricature of characters
Think as you read: what Pancake is; who the office boy was and why he was frustrated; why the author was thought to do nothing
Understanding the text: how the author creates humour; Subbu as a many-sided genius; the legal adviser and the actress
Why the English poet's visit was a mystery; what 'The God That Failed' was
Talking about the text: humour as a tool; the place of poetry in films
Short answers on Subbu, the MRA visit and Spender; long answer on humour in the text
Part I: Christopher Silvester's introduction to 'The Penguin Book of Interviews' on the history and views of interviews
Part II: extract from Mukund Padmanabhan's interview with Umberto Eco in The Hindu

sections.name: 7.2 Part I: The interview as a form

concepts.text: The interview was invented a little over 130 years ago and is now a commonplace of journalism
Positive view: an art and a source of truth; the interviewer holds great power and influence
Negative view: an intrusion into private lives that diminishes celebrities
Some primitive cultures believe a photograph steals the soul; V.S. Naipaul felt interviews wound people and take away part of them
Lewis Carroll had a 'defensive dread' of interviewers and never agreed to be interviewed
Rudyard Kipling called the interview immoral, a crime, an assault deserving punishment
Kipling's wife wrote that reporters from Boston ruined their day
H.G. Wells called it an 'ordeal' but later himself interviewed Joseph Stalin
Saul Bellow described interviews as thumbprints on his windpipe
Denis Brian: we learn most about our contemporaries through interviews
Eco: Italian professor of semiotics (study of signs) at the University of Bologna
Scholarly works on semiotics, literary interpretation and medieval aesthetics, plus essays and novels
'The Name of the Rose' (1980), a medieval detective novel, sold 10 to 15 million copies
He works in 'interstices': small empty spaces of time between tasks
He uses a playful, narrative, non-academic style even in scholarly writing
He calls himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays
He thinks the novel's success is a mystery; it might not have sold ten years earlier or later
Readers liked its medieval setting and serious content despite its difficulty
Interviews: art versus intrusion; the power of the interviewer
Creativity and the efficient use of time
Popularity, scholarship and fiction
Expository prose with quotations (Part I); question-answer interview format (Part II)
Metaphors: thumbprints on the windpipe; 'interstices'
Understanding the text: positive and negative views of interviews; why celebrity writers despise being interviewed
The belief about photographs in primitive cultures; meaning of 'thumbprints on his windpipe'
Who is lionised today and why; Eco's 'interstices'; why Eco's academic writing is personal and playful
How Eco explains the success of 'The Name of the Rose'
Talking about the text: the interview as a form of journalism
Things to do: plan questions and conduct an interview
Short answers on views on interviews and Eco; long answer on the interview as a medium

sections.name: 8.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: A.R. Barton: writer of this story of adolescent fantasy in a working-class English family
Third-person narration focused on Sophie's thoughts
Sophie and Jansie are school-leavers likely to end up working at the biscuit factory
Sophie dreams of opening a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer
Jansie is practical and reminds her such plans need money and experience
At home: her father (a manual worker), tired mother, older brother Geoff and little brother Derek
Sophie admires Geoff, an apprentice mechanic who keeps his life private
She tells Geoff she met Danny Casey, the young Irish football star, in the arcade
She claims Casey promised to meet her by the canal; Geoff and her father do not believe her
On Saturday the family watches United play; Casey scores a goal
Sophie waits by the canal near a tree, but Casey never comes
She goes home sad but still clings to the fantasy and fears others will learn the truth
Sophie: dreamy, romantic, escapist, longing for glamour
Jansie: realistic and gossipy; Sophie fears she will spread the story
Geoff: silent, reserved, with a world of his own
Father: hard-working, sceptical football fan; mother: tired and anxious
Adolescent fantasy and hero worship
Dreams versus reality and the limits of class
Communication gaps within the family
Irony of the title 'Going Places' against Sophie's limited prospects
Contrast between Sophie and Jansie; the canal meeting as a symbol of illusion
Think as you read: where Sophie wants to work; why Jansie discourages her; why Sophie admires Geoff
Understanding the text: Sophie's fantasy world; why she waits by the canal; significance of the title
Talking about the text: hero worship among teenagers; dreams that cannot come true
Short answers on Sophie and Geoff; long answer on fantasy versus reality

sections.name: 9.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Kamala Das: Indian poet writing in English and Malayalam, known for confessional poetry
A short autobiographical poem written as one long sentence without stanza breaks
The poet drives from her parents' home to Cochin airport on a Friday morning
Her mother sits beside her, dozing with her mouth open
The mother's face looks ashen like a corpse; the poet realises with pain that her mother is old
She turns away to look at young trees sprinting and merry children spilling out of their homes
At the airport security check she looks again: her mother is wan and pale as a late winter's moon
An old childhood fear of losing her mother returns as an ache
She hides her feelings and says only 'See you soon, Amma'
She smiles and smiles and smiles to reassure her mother
Ageing of a parent and the fear of separation and death
Contrast between youth and old age, life and decay
Love, helplessness and suppressed emotion
Simile: face ashen like a corpse; pale as a late winter's moon
Imagery: young trees sprinting, merry children spilling out
Personification: the sprinting trees
Repetition: 'smile and smile and smile'
Contrast between inside the car (age) and outside (youth); enjambment; free verse
The kind of pain and ache the poet feels
Why the young trees are described as sprinting
Why the poet brings in the image of merry children
Why the mother is compared to a late winter's moon
What the parting words and the smile signify
Extract-based MCQs on similes and contrast; short answers on the poet's fear

sections.name: 10.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Pablo Neruda: Chilean poet and diplomat, Nobel Prize in Literature (1971)
Translated from Spanish (Alastair Reid); free verse
Let us count to twelve and keep still, all over the earth, for once
No one would speak any language; we would not move our arms
An exotic moment without rush or engines, all together in a sudden strangeness
Fishermen in the cold sea would not harm whales
The man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands
Those preparing green wars, wars with gas and fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk with their brothers
The poet does not want total inactivity; life is what it is all about
If we were not so single-minded about keeping busy, a huge silence might end our sadness of never understanding ourselves
The earth teaches us: when everything seems dead, it later proves to be alive
Ending: the poet counts to twelve, asks us to keep quiet, and leaves
Silence, introspection and self-understanding
Universal brotherhood, peace and non-violence
Criticism of war, harm to nature and mindless activity
Anaphora and repetition; imagery of fishermen, whales and the salt gatherer
Personification of the earth; paradox of life under apparent death
Free verse and direct address to the reader
What counting to twelve and keeping still will help us achieve
Whether the poet advocates total inactivity and death
What 'sadness' the poet refers to
The symbol from nature showing life under apparent stillness
Lines that best convey the poet's message
Extract-based MCQs; short answers on introspection and peace

sections.name: 11.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: John Keats: English Romantic poet; lines from the opening of the long poem 'Endymion'
Written in rhyming (heroic) couplets in iambic pentameter
A thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness
It keeps a quiet bower for us, and sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing
Every morning we weave a flowery band to bind us to the earth
Beauty helps in spite of despondence, the dearth of noble natures, gloomy days and unhealthy ways
Some shape of beauty removes the pall from our dark spirits
Things of beauty: sun, moon, trees old and young giving shade to simple sheep, daffodils and their green world
Clear rills that make a cooling covert, the mid-forest brake with musk-rose blooms
The grandeur of dooms imagined for the mighty dead; lovely tales heard or read
An endless fountain of immortal drink pouring to us from heaven's brink
Beauty gives lasting joy and makes life bearable
Nature's healing power against suffering
Beauty as a divine gift that binds us to the earth
Metaphors: flowery band, pall, endless fountain of immortal drink
Nature imagery; alliteration; inversion
Rhyming couplets and Romantic diction
List the things of beauty mentioned in the poem
List the things that cause suffering and pain
What 'wreathing a flowery band to bind us to the earth' suggests
What makes human beings love life despite troubles
Why 'grandeur' is linked with the 'mighty dead'
Whether things of beauty make a lasting impression
The image used for the bounty of the earth
Extract-based MCQs; short answers on nature and beauty

sections.name: 12.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Robert Frost: American poet of rural New England
A narrative-reflective poem on the plight of the rural poor beside a highway
A little old house has a shed at the road's edge where farmers sell to passers-by
They want a share of city money to live better, like city people
The polished traffic passes with its mind ahead; if anyone looks, it is to complain
Complaint: the crudely painted signs (N and S turned wrong) spoil the landscape
Goods offered: wild berries in wooden quarts, crook-necked golden squash with silver warts, and a beautiful mountain scene
The poet's real complaint is the trusting sorrow of what is left unsaid
News that these 'pitiful kin' will be bought out and gathered into villages near theatre and store
'Greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey' swarm over their lives with unwanted benefits
The rural folk wait all day for the squeal of brakes; cars stop only to turn round, ask the way, or ask for a gallon of gas
The poet sometimes wishes to put them out of their pain at once, then wonders how he would feel if someone did that to him
Rural poverty and the indifference of the urban rich
Hypocrisy of welfare planners and agencies
The poet's empathy and helplessness
Oxymoron 'beneficent beasts of prey'; alliteration 'greedy good-doers'
Irony and sarcasm; imagery of the stand and the polished traffic
Rhyming lines with varied length
Lines showing city folk ignoring or complaining about the stand, and what their complaint was
The plea of the people who set up the stand
Words showing the double standards of government and social agencies
What the 'childish longing' is and why it is in vain
Lines showing the poet's pain at the plight of the rural poor
Extract-based MCQs; short answers on urban indifference and false welfare

sections.name: 13.1 About the poet and the poem

concepts.text: Adrienne Rich: American poet and feminist
Three quatrains in rhyming couplets (aabb)
Aunt Jennifer's tigers prance across a screen (her embroidery panel)
They are bright topaz denizens of a world of green
They do not fear the men beneath the tree; they pace in sleek chivalric certainty
Her fingers flutter through the wool; even the ivory needle is hard to pull
The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band sits heavily on her hand
When she is dead, her terrified hands will still lie ringed with the ordeals she was mastered by
The tigers she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid
Oppression of women in patriarchal marriage
Art as escape and self-expression; art outlives the artist
Contrast between the fearless tigers and the timid aunt
Symbolism: tigers (freedom, courage), wedding band (bondage), ivory needle
Colour imagery (topaz, green); alliteration (prance, proud)
Irony: a fearful woman creates fearless creatures
How 'denizens' and 'chivalric' add to our understanding of the tigers
Why her fingers flutter and the needle is hard to pull
What the 'massive weight of Uncle's wedding band' suggests
What Aunt Jennifer is terrified of
Significance of the tigers prancing even after her death
Why she created animals so unlike herself; interpreting the symbols
Extract-based MCQs on symbols; short answers on oppression

sections.name: 14.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Jack Finney: American writer of science fiction and fantasy
First-person narration by Charley; blends realism with fantasy and time travel
Charley, 31, insists Grand Central Station in New York has three levels, though officials say two
Taking a short cut through the station, he gets lost and reaches a third level
It has gas lights, brass spittoons, old-fashioned clothes, derby hats and sideburns, and an old Currier and Ives-style locomotive
A newspaper, 'The World', is dated 11 June 1894
He tries to buy two tickets to Galesburg, Illinois, a peaceful town of that era
The clerk rejects his modern money and suspects him; he hurries away
He withdraws $300 and exchanges it for old-style currency, getting less than $200 worth
He can never find the corridor to the third level again
Psychiatrist friend Sam Weiner calls it a waking-dream wish fulfilment, an escape from insecurity and fear
Stamp collecting is also described as a temporary refuge from reality
Sam disappears; Charley finds in his grandfather's stamp collection a first-day cover postmarked 18 July 1894, written by Sam from Galesburg
Sam had set up a hay, feed and grain business there and urged Charley and his wife Louisa to keep looking
Charley: imaginative and anxious, longing for a simpler past
Louisa: Charley's supportive wife
Sam Weiner: the psychiatrist who rationalises, yet himself escapes into the past
Escapism from modern insecurity, war and worry
Fantasy versus reality; the intersection of time and space
Nostalgia for a peaceful past
First-person narration; irony (the psychiatrist escapes); Grand Central compared to a growing tree
Twist ending with the first-day cover as evidence
Was the third level a medium of escape for Charley?
What Sam's letter suggests about the reality of the third level
Is there an intersection of time and space in the story?
Can the past be relived? discuss
Significance of first-day covers and stamp collecting
Short answers on Charley's experience; long answer on escapism

sections.name: 15.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Kalki (R. Krishnamurthy): Tamil writer and journalist known for satire
A satire on the vanity of rulers and the destruction of wildlife
Maharaja Sir Jilani Jung Jung Bahadur of Pratibandapuram is called the Tiger King
At his birth astrologers foretold he would die because of a tiger
The ten-day-old prince miraculously spoke and warned that tigers should beware
He was raised by an English nurse and tutor; at twenty he became king
He killed his first tiger and vowed to kill a hundred; the astrologer warned him about the hundredth
He banned tiger hunting by anyone else in his state
A high-ranking British officer wanted to hunt a tiger; the king refused and risked losing his throne
He saved his kingdom by sending about fifty costly diamond rings to the officer's wife
Within ten years he killed seventy tigers; tigers vanished from his state
He married a girl from a state with many tigers and killed tigers there on each visit
After ninety-nine tigers, the dewan secretly brought an old tiger from the People's Park in Madras
The king's bullet missed; the tiger fainted from shock and the hunters killed it secretly
For his son's third birthday he bought a cheap wooden toy tiger; a sliver pierced his hand
The infection spread and he died during surgery: the hundredth tiger had its revenge
The Maharaja: vain, stubborn, proud of his power
The dewan: fearful but cunning; the chief astrologer: prophetic
Satire on royalty, arrogance and abuse of power
Irony of fate and the inevitability of destiny
Destruction of wildlife and the need for conservation
Satire, irony and dramatic irony
Humour and exaggeration; suspense around the hundredth tiger
Irony in the story and how it builds suspense
How the writer satirises those in power

concepts.text: Tishani Doshi: Indian poet, journalist and dancer
Travel account of a visit to Antarctica with the 'Students on Ice' programme
She travels from Madras across nine time zones, six checkpoints, three bodies of water and three ecospheres
The voyage is aboard the Russian research vessel 'Akademik Shokalskiy'
Antarctica: coldest, driest, windiest continent, holding about 90 per cent of the earth's ice
About 650 million years ago the supercontinent Gondwana was centred near present-day Antarctica
Gondwana broke up and the continents drifted to their present positions
Antarctica's ice preserves a record of the earth's past
Melting of the West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea levels dramatically
Rising carbon dioxide, global warming and ozone depletion threaten the planet
Phytoplankton ('grasses of the sea') feed the whole Southern Ocean food chain through photosynthesis
Small changes can have large effects: take care of small things and big things will follow

sections.name: 17.1 About the author and the text

concepts.text: Pearl S. Buck: American writer, Nobel Prize in Literature (1938)
Set in Japan during the Second World War
Dr Sadao Hoki, a Japanese surgeon trained in America, lives in a house on the Japanese coast with his wife Hana
His father had valued education; Sadao met Hana in America
In the mist they find a wounded white man washed ashore; his cap reads 'U.S. Navy'
He is an escaped American prisoner of war with a gunshot wound
Sadao and Hana are torn between patriotism and humanity; they take him in
The servants disapprove, refuse to help and later leave the house
Sadao operates and removes the bullet; Hana washes and feeds the man
Sadao is called to treat the ailing General and confesses about the American
The General promises to send private assassins, then forgets, absorbed in his own health
Sadao helps the American escape by boat with food, water and a flashlight for signalling
The American gets away; Sadao wonders why he could not kill him
Dr Sadao: dedicated surgeon torn between nationalism and humanity
Hana: compassionate, supportive wife
The General: self-centred and pragmatic
Humanity above patriotism and prejudice

sections.name: 18.1 About the author and the play

concepts.text: Susan Hill: English novelist and playwright; a one-act play in two scenes
Characters: Derry (a boy of about fourteen), Mr Lamb (an old man) and Derry's mother
Derry climbs into Mr Lamb's garden thinking it empty; Mr Lamb welcomes him
Derry's face was burnt by acid; he is bitter and withdrawn
Mr Lamb has a tin leg, lost in a war; children call him 'Lamey-Lamb'
The garden: crab apples for jelly, bees and honey, weeds and flowers
Mr Lamb's philosophy: all things in nature are equal; people fear what is different
Derry recalls hearing his mother say only a mother could love such a face
Mr Lamb tells of a man who shut himself away in fear and died anyway
Derry promises to return to help pick crab apples
Derry's mother forbids him to go back to Mr Lamb
Derry insists he wants to go out and see the world
Derry returns to find Mr Lamb has fallen from the ladder and died; he weeps
Derry: bitter and insecure, but learns hope
Mr Lamb: wise, cheerful, lonely and accepting

Two autobiographical episodes by women from marginalised communities
Part 1 by Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin), Native American writer; Part 2 by Bama, Tamil Dalit writer (from 'Karukku')

sections.name: 19.2 Part 1: The Cutting of My Long Hair

concepts.text: Zitkala-Sa recalls her first day at a missionary boarding school for Native American children
Strict rules: bells, marching, eating by formula; she felt embarrassed and watched
Her friend Judewin warned that the authorities would cut their long hair
In her culture short (shingled) hair marked cowards or mourners
She hid under a bed in a dark room but was found and dragged out
She was tied to a chair and her long hair was cut; she felt like an animal driven by a herder
She lost her spirit; no one comforted her

sections.name: 19.3 Part 2: We Too Are Human Beings

concepts.text: Bama, in the third grade, walks home slowly watching the street sights
She sees an elder of her community carrying a packet of vadai by its string so as not to touch it
She finds it funny at first; her brother Annan explains untouchability and caste
Annan advises her to study hard because education earns respect
She studies hard and stands first in her class
Cultural oppression and loss of identity
